sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Radagast** ​(*radagast*) — ‌Hospitality, Animals ‌· ​Council of ​the gods ​— ​belongs to ​the Slavic ‌tradition, ​where it ​is ‌catalogued under ​the domain ‌"Hospitality, ​Animals". The ‌name means ​"Council ​of the ​gods"[^1].

**Radagast** ​— ​medieval *Radigost* ‌— was ​the ‌chief god ​of the ‌Redarii, ​a Slavic ‌people ​between the ‌Elbe and ​the ​Oder, worshipped ‌in a ‌great ‌wooden temple-city ​called Radgosc. ​His ‌name ties ​him to ​the ‌guest and ​the glad ​welcome: ‌he is ​the ‌god of ​hospitality, of ​the ​open door, ​of beasts, ‌and ‌of the ​trust between ‌strangers.[^2]

​PuniCodex records ​the canonical ‌scholarly ‌spelling **Radagast** ‌and serves ‌its ​temple at ‌[its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/radagast/). The ​displayed form ​is ‌ASCII-equivalent — ​a description ​computed ​from the ‌displayed form ​itself. ​The plain ​ASCII form ‌*radagast* ​contains the ‌same letters: ​no ‌recovered diacritics ​or ‌special encoding ‌is claimed. ​The ​work here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation ‌survives for ​this ​name; **Radagast** ​is ​a scholarly ​transliteration ‌of the ​reconstructed ​spoken ‌form. Etymologically ​the ‌name means ​"Council ‌of the ​gods"[^1].

​The canonical ​spelling ​**Radagast** matches ​the ‌conventional scholarly ​romanization. ‌The plain ​ASCII ‌form *radagast* ​contains ‌the same ​letters, ‌so no ​lost ​diacritics or ‌encoding ‌transition ‌is claimed. ​The ​editorial work ‌is ​to fix ​one ‌reviewed reference ​spelling, ​preserve capitalization ‌and ​provenance, and ‌keep ​the original ​evidence ​visible. The ​displayed ‌form is ‌ASCII-equivalent ​— a ‌description ​computed ​from the ‌displayed ‌form itself.

‌The ‌letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ‌**r** → ​**R** ​— Same
- ​**a** ‌→ **a** ​— ​Same
- **d** ​→ ‌**d** — ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/radagast/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**radagast** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Radagast.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Radagast" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Radagast" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"radagast" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Radagast ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Radagast ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Radagast ‌place ​hospitality, animals ​at ​the ​center of ​a ‌living ​mythological world.

### ​Origins ‌(Myth)

Radagast ​appears ‌in ​slavic tradition ‌as ​hospitality, ​animals. The ​name's ​meaning, ​"Council of ‌the ​gods", shapes ‌the ​narratives ‌told about ​this ‌figure.

### ​Worship and ‌Memory ​(Cult)

​Devotees and ‌later ‌tradition-keepers preserved ‌Radagast ​in ​ritual, text, ‌and ​iconography, ​ensuring the ‌name ​survived ​into the ‌modern ​scholarly record.

‌The ​myths ​of Radagast ​survive ​in ‌fragments, summaries, ‌and ​later ‌retellings. Each ​version ​reflects the ‌interests ‌of ‌its tellers ‌— ​poets, ‌priests, philosophers, ​and ​scholars. ​The PuniCodex ‌entry ​does not ​privilege ​a ‌single version; ​it ​gathers ​the attestations ‌so ​that ‌readers can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌Radagast ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Radagast ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Slavic ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Radagast, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​hospitality ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Radagast ​is the ‌patron of ‌everything we ​almost lost. ​His entire ​dossier comes ​from men ​who wanted ‌him gone ​— a ​bishop, ‌two monks, ​writing the ‌god into ​extinction — ‌and yet ​the name ​refused to ​die, surfacing ​three centuries ​later on ‌the ​lips of ‌a fantasy ​writer who ‌liked its ​sound. There ‌is a ​lesson in ‌that: worship ​is louder ​than witnesses, ‌and ‌a god ‌of hospitality ​is especially ​hard to ‌kill, because ​hospitality is ​the one ‌divine office ​every culture ​keeps open.

‌He ​also asks ‌an uncomfortable ​question of ​the scholarly ​record. When ​a people's ‌own voices ‌are silenced, ​what remains ‌is the ​enemies' ​paperwork — ‌and we ‌build temples ‌of the ‌imagination on ​it anyway. ‌Radagast's temple ​is real ​now precisely ​because it ‌is ​contested: nobody's ​property, everybody's ​guest. That, ‌in the ​end, is ​the meaning ​of his ‌name. The ​god who ‌gladly receives ​survives ‌by being ​received — ‌by chroniclers, ‌by philologists, ​by children ​who never ​heard of ​the Redarii ‌and love ‌the wizard ​anyway.[^1]
